text: Every integration you've built so far — REST Messages, the Table API, IntegrationHub spoke actions — assumed the system on the other end has a public URL the ServiceNow instance can reach directly. That assumption holds for a SaaS vendor's API. It breaks completely for an internal database, a legacy on-prem application, a network device, or a monitoring tool sitting behind a corporate firewall.

ServiceNow's instance runs in ServiceNow's own cloud. Internal enterprise systems routinely have no public-facing endpoint at all, by design — that's exactly what a firewall is for. There's no URL for the cloud instance to call, because nothing behind that firewall is reachable from the public internet. That's the real gap this chapter solves.

A MID Server — Management, Instrumentation, and Discovery — is a real, lightweight Java application. The customer downloads it from their instance and installs it on a machine they own: on-premises, or inside their own cloud VPC. It shows up on the instance as a MID Server record, reporting its status and version, but it runs entirely on the customer's own infrastructure, not ServiceNow's.

Here's the detail that makes it all work: a MID Server makes outbound-only connections from inside the customer's network back out to the ServiceNow instance, polling on a short interval for work to do. The instance never initiates a connection into the customer's network — the MID Server always reaches outward first.

That outbound-only design is the real security property that makes MID Servers acceptable in security-conscious enterprises: the customer never has to open an inbound firewall port. Every security team's default posture is a firewall closed to inbound traffic, and a MID Server never asks them to break that rule. Next, Lesson 25 covers exactly what work gets routed through one.
